conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to see how you’ve been coping over the past seven days. It’s simply ten short questions; your answers stay private and help us figure out what extra support—if any—might help you feel more like yourself. There are no right or wrong answers, only what’s true for you. Ready to start?

First, how often in the past week have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, not very often. I do manage to laugh a little when my husband makes a joke or when the baby does something cute, but it feels forced—like I’m doing it because I know I should, not because it feels natural. Most of the time, it’s hard to find anything really funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes, yes… but it feels kind of hollow, like I’m pretending. I’ll smile if my husband makes a joke or if the baby does something cute, but the laugh doesn’t last, and I go right back to feeling heavy.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I still go through the motions—like I’ll plan to meet a friend for coffee or sit down to watch a show I used to love—but when the time comes, I don’t feel that spark. It’s like I remember I *should* be excited, but mostly I just feel flat or wonder if it’s even worth the effort.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty often. If the baby fusses for a long time, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a bad mom.” I know rationally it’s not always my fault, but the guilty thought pops up anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… a lot of the time. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly worry her breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie down and picture the stroller tipping even though it’s locked. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just race and I can’t shut them off for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes… like the other night I was just rocking her in the nursery and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt I couldn’t catch my breath. Nothing had happened—no noise, no fever—just this wave of “what if something’s wrong?” It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days it feels like I’m barely treading water. The laundry, the dishes, the feeding schedule—individually they’re small, but together they feel like a wave that keeps knocking me over. I manage to get through each task, but it’s overwhelming and I end the day exhausted and teary.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t settle. I keep replaying every little thing I did with the baby—did I burp her long enough, did I fasten the car seat right—and then I’m wide-awake for an hour or two. When I finally drift off, I wake up again with my heart pounding for no clear reason.
I have felt sad or miserable

A good bit of the time… it’s like a cloud that settles over me. I’ll be holding her and feel this heaviness in my chest, or I’ll look at her tiny face and instead of pure joy I feel guilty for not feeling happier. I’m not crying all day, but the sadness lingers in the background most of the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s usually once or twice a week. The other night she wouldn’t settle and I just sat on the couch with her on my shoulder and started crying—quietly, so she wouldn’t hear. It’s like the pressure builds up and the tears sneak out before I can stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

I… I’ve had a couple of quick thoughts, like wondering if everyone would be better off without me, but I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to leave her. They’re just flashes that scare me, and I push them away as fast as they come.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today’s date]  
Source: self-report  

### Primary symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, sadness “most of the time”  
- Markedly reduced pleasure/interest in usual activities  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt (“bad mom” cognitions)  
- Recurrent, intrusive worries and nocturnal rumination  
- Episodic panic-type symptoms (sudden racing heart, breathlessness)  
- Frequent crying (≈ 1–2×/wk)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulty linked to anxious ruminations  
- Daily sense of being overwhelmed and “treading water”  

### Pattern  
Symptoms present most days for ≥ past 2 weeks; fluctuate through day, worsen evenings; interfere with infant care and self-care.  

### Screening significance  
Findings exceed “baby blues” threshold; meet core criteria for probable **major depressive episode with peripartum onset** and comorbid **anxiety symptoms**.  

### Risk factors / red flags  
- Pervasive anhedonia  
- Negative maternal self-appraisal  
- Panic-equivalent episodes  
- Passive self-harm ideation (no plan/intent) – **safety item identified**  

### Safety  
Patient denies intent or plan; protective factors (strong infant attachment, supportive husband). Agreed to notify provider or emergency services if thoughts escalate.  

### Screening summary  
High likelihood of moderate–severe postpartum depression with anxious features; rule-out formal diagnosis and safety plan recommended.
